newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: FEDERAL CABINET LIKELY TO DISCUSS WIK RESPONSE TODAY

Aboriginal leaders have presented their final submission to the Prime Minister on the Wik decision, as the Federal Cabinet prepares to discuss its response to the High Court judgement in Brisbane today.
Aboriginal representatives have signalled they will strongly oppose any move to extinguish native title rights, which John Howard has not ruled out.
Other options Mr Howard is expected to brief his colleagues on include legislation to spell out the rights of pastoralists.
Queensland National Party MP's have warned of a Coalition split on the issue of extinguishment.
Meanwhile, Australia's Ambassador to Iran, Stuart Hume, will brief Foreign Affairs Minister, Alexander Downer, in Brisbane today, after being recalled in protest against Iran's terrorist activities.
UNION SAYS CONTRACTORS MAY CONTRIBUTE TO MINE ACCIDENTS
The Australian Workers Union says the use of contractors on mines in the Goldfields may be contributing to industry accidents.
The claim follows the death of mine worker 47 year old Peter Martin Able at Western Mining's Victor mine at Kambalda on Sunday.
Union representative Henry Rosmianiec says contractors are under enormous pressure to perform and this may lead to an increased margin for error.
Mr Rosmeniac says he's concerned the tragedy occurred so close to a rock fall in February in which three miners were lucky to escape serious injury at the nearby Long mine.
Both mines are owned by Western Mining and staffed by Eltin contractors.
Meanwhile, the company was yesterday fined A$60,000 in the Kalgoorlie Magistrate's Court for failing to provide a safe working place.
The company admitted a charge which was laid when an underground miner was killed in a rockfall at Kambalda last year.
WESTERN AUSTRALIA CRITICISES COMMONWEALTH FUNDING
Western Australia's Finance Minister, Max Evans, says the State is not getting the full benefit of its booming economy because of Commonwealth tax sharing arrangements and Federal grants.
Mr Evans has written a letter urging his Federal counterparts to lobby the Commonwealth about an imbalance in the finacial arrangements between the States.
The Minister sent a similar letter to Coalition members of the WA Parliament last week.
He says Western Australia's tremendous economic progress is enriching the Federal Government, but the State isn't getting its fair share back.
Mr Evans says Federal funding to the State has dropped by more than A$5 million dollars over the last four years.
FOOD POISONING AT INDONESIAN FESTIVAL IN VICTORIA
Victoria's Department of Human Services says the number of people affected by the state's latest food poisoning outbreak could rise.
So far 19 people have reported severe gastro enteritis after attending an Indonesian Festival at the Malvern Town Hall in Melbourne.
Seventeen of them have been treated at hospital and five admitted. But health authorities says 120 people ate the same food.
Updated figures on the numbers affected by the outbreak will be released today.
The Festival was organised by the Indonesian Students Association.
INSURANCE COUNCIL WORRIED ABOUT RATE OF COVER IN REGIONS
The Insurance Council of Australia is concerned about a high proportion of people in regional area who're not insuring their building or contents.
The problem has been highlighted by an analysis of major storm damage in Coffs Harbour last year.

Insurance Council spokesman Chris Henry says the council found about 67 percent of the contents of homes affected by the storm were not insured and about 45 percent of homes affected were not insured.
Mr Henry says nationally about 20 percent of all contents are uninsured and about nine percent of homes are not insured.
He says some people think they can't afford insurance while others think they'll never need insurance coverage.
SCIENTIST SAYS ANTI-SCIENTIFIC MOVEMENT GROWING
Renowned scientist, author and broadcaster Karl Kruszelnicki says more people are adopting anti-scientific ideas about medicine.
Dr Kruszelnicki, best known for his Great Moments in Science' book and radio series was speaking at the opening of National Science Week in Sydney last night.
He says while growing numbers of people now understand the critical role of science, the anti-scientific movement has also gathered momentum.
Dr Kruszelnicki says more people are going for what he calls the rubbish that anti-biotics are not needed, and a few crystals will suffice.
Another myth he says is that aromatherapy can fix total paralysis.
